parts: Text prepared for publication in "EL Mundo del Perro" magazine, No. 357, small breeds special: Shih Tzu
Author: Yolanda Berdugo
ORIGINS OF THE BREED

The Shih Tzu's ancestry dates back to 1000 BC and is Tibetan in origin. The history of the Tibetan "lion dog" is intertwined with Buddhism, which originated in India. Lions were closely associated with Buddhism, but were not native to China, so the Chinese and Tibetan lamas bred their dogs to resemble lions. The Shih Tzu, whose name means lion, may have been the oldest and smallest variety of the "sacred dogs" and shares certain similarities with other Tibetan breeds. Throughout much of China's long and illustrious history, breeding the little "lion dog" was a favourite pastime of imperial rulers.

The exact origins of the Shih Tzu remain shrouded in mystery, although Lamaism offers some clues. Maujusri, the lama deity of learning, was often accompanied by a small dog capable of turning into a lion. With its own leonine appearance, the Tibetan Lhasa Apso became closely associated with this lion dog. Chinese emperors regularly received Lhasa Apsos as gifts from Tibet's ruler, the Dalai Lama. It therefore seems likely that, once in China, these exotic dogs were crossed with Pekingese to create the breed we know today.

Documents show that, before AD 624, these small dogs were exported from Malta, Turkey, Greece and Persia as gifts to the Chinese emperors. The first Tibetan lion dog, from which the Shih Tzu probably descended, is believed to have reached China during the Qing (Ch'ing) dynasty as tribute from the Grand Lamas to the Chinese Empire.
HISTORY AS TOLD BY A SHIH TZU

Our name means "Lion Dog", and we are one of the four recognised breeds of Tibetan origin. It is known that the Dalai Lama gave us to Chinese royal families as a sign of good fortune and luck. We were an important gift because Tibetans believed that the "Snow Lioness", a mythological creature with a prominent place in local lore, was reincarnated in us. This also explains why such a tiny animal was called a "Lion Dog".
Although the beginnings of our breeding are somewhat lost in time, some say our origins date back to 1,000 BC.
The first documented evidence of our existence, however, dates from the 7th century, as we appear on various objects and in paintings from the Tang dynasty (618-907).

We appear again in paintings and objects dating from 990 to 994, but do not reappear in written records until the 13th century. Marco Polo then wrote that "Emperor Kubla Khan kept small 'lion dogs' alongside lions trained for hunting. The dogs were not food for the lions, but companions that kept them calm when they were not hunting".

During the Ming dynasty (1368-1644), we were favourites of the Chinese royal families, who entrusted our breeding to eunuchs. Several documents state that "the little lion dogs, or chrysanthemum-faced dogs, were small, intelligent, gentle and unmistakably lion-like". We were protected for life, accorded high honours and given the finest care. We lived in the best part of the palace and ate food from the emperor's own table.
The lion dog pagoda is said to have been used by the eunuchs "to exercise the little lion dogs of the Imperial Palace".
So, as you can see, the mysteries of Tibet and the secrets of the Forbidden City lie at the origins of our breed.
However, we owe the Shih Tzu we know today to Empress Regent Cixi (T'zu Hsi), who devoted herself to breeding and refining the court's three Chinese breeds during her regency (1861-1908).

The empress asked the court's dog breeders for "a sociable companion dog that seldom barked, with a long coat to warm one's hands and a silent gait". This is how we modern Shih Tzu came into being, as an "Imperial Dog that should never leave the walls of the Forbidden City".

And that was almost the case. British residents in China repeatedly tried to take us to England in the early 20th century, mostly without success. The eunuchs who cared for us did not want us to leave the country. Court etiquette considered it very impolite to say "no" to a request, so when members of the British community asked to acquire some dogs, they were offered them with a friendly smile. Yet the dogs died within days. The eunuchs were forbidden to let Shih Tzu leave China, so they fed them crushed glass before handing them over to their new owners. The dogs then bled to death aboard the ships returning to the British Isles.

The first record of us being in Western hands concerns a gift from Empress Cixi to Mrs Kaufmann, wife of the Danish consul in China and a friend of the empress. She was gifted a pair, Leidza and Aidzo, marking the beginning of Western breeding of our breed.

In 1908, Empress Cixi (T'zu Hsi), mother of Pu'Yi, the Last Emperor, died. Breeding virtually ceased, continuing only through the efforts of a few private individuals and other members of the court. The breed finally became extinct in China with the arrival of communism.

In 1928, Lady Brownrigg brought a pair to England: Shu-ssa, the female, and Hibou, the male. Later, in 1933, Mrs Hutchins took another male, Lung-fu-ssa, to Ireland. A few more followed from Bejing, bringing the total to around ten. It is fair to say that all of us Shih Tzu today descend from these dogs.
The only female who genuinely came from the Imperial Chinese court arrived in Norway.
Gradually, over the decades, we became one of the most popular and cherished breeds in the world.

When we arrived in Europe, we were registered as "Apsos". Then the "war of the noses" began, because our muzzles are shorter than those of the Apsos. Finally, in 1934, the two breeds were officially separated, at least in Great Britain. In the United States, we were not officially recognised as a separate breed until 1969.

Over the years, our breed spread throughout the world. Today, we are equally happy in palaces or castles, on the 25th or 37th floor, or in a sunny house with a garden. We adapt easily to the surroundings in which our dear human friends live. If, for some particular reason, our owners can no longer care for us, we give all our affection to those who take their place, without ever forgetting those who first gave us love and a home.

Every dog is known to have a purpose. Our main purpose in life is to offer love, companionship and the pleasure of seeing our noble heritage reflected in our elegant gait. We are sincere creatures, not suited to hunting, fighting or attacking. We simply want to give and receive love and affection, hoping to charm with our beauty, proud bearing and distinction. For this reason, we are classified as companion dogs in Europe, as Toy, Luxury and Companion dogs in the United States, as Non-Sporting dogs in Australia and as Utility dogs in the United Kingdom.
HISTORY

Their ancestors were bred for the pleasure and pride of emperors, playing and running through palaces on gleaming marble floors or resting on beautiful satin cushions. The name Shih-Tzu, given to the breed, means Lion Dog of Tibet. This does not mean they were bred to hunt lions, but rather that, when trimmed and groomed, they resemble miniature lions. At the time, the same name was given to Pekingese, Lhasa Apsos and possibly Japanese Spaniels and Pugs.

Regarding their origins, during the Manchu dynasty, founded in 1583, it was customary for Tibet's Dalai Lama to send the finest Lhasa Apsos as gifts to the powerful emperor of China. Perhaps for this reason, Manchu generals returning triumphant from invasions of Tibet during the 18th century adopted the custom of bringing back Lhasa Apsos as spoils of war. These dogs were ceremoniously placed at the emperor's feet as symbols of Manchu victories by the officers who had played the most important roles in those wars. Crossbreeding these Lhasas with native Chinese Pekingese in the royal palaces gave rise to the "Shih-Tzu" breed, as did crosses with other so-called lion dogs with short muzzles and rather flat faces. Whether this was intentional is unknown, and it occurred on a greater scale than might have been imagined. Their beauty and temperament contributed to the breed's rapid growth. The original lion dogs, and especially their ancestors, were protected for life, accorded high honours and carefully tended, living in the finest quarters and eating food from the emperor's own table.

In 1920, the first pair of Shih Tzu, pronounced Shid Zoo, was brought to England. Further imports followed, and the breed became firmly established there. Its popularity spread to continental Europe and North America, where it now enjoys an enormous following.

Over the years, the breed spread throughout the world. Today, these dogs are equally happy in palaces or castles, on the 25th or 37th floor of a modern skyscraper, in a modest flat or in a sunny house with a garden. They adapt easily to the surroundings in which their dear human friends live. If, for some particular reason, their owners can no longer care for them, they give all their affection to those who take their place, without ever forgetting those who first gave them love and a home.

Every dog is known to have a purpose. Their main purpose in life is to offer love, companionship and the pleasure of seeing their ancient noble lineage reflected in their elegant gait. They are sincere creatures, not suited to hunting, fighting or attacking. They simply want to give and receive love and affection, hoping to charm with their beauty, proud bearing and distinction. For this reason, they are included in the "Toy, Luxury and Companion" group.
The Shih Tzu is classified as a Non-Sporting dog in Australia, a Toy in the United States and a Utility dog in the United Kingdom.
